rationale: A wins because it gives the founder three real editorial doors: retail strategy, ESG credentialing, and finance. Its best move, “The canned water brand that named its store 'Country Club' just earned a B Corp certification,” finds a live tension without pretending there is a new product. B has one strong channel angle, but “Liquid Death's first store sells T-shirts, limited-run cans and event tickets — not a new product” invents ticket sales and sits too close to “Already in 120,000 stores, Liquid Death is opening one of its own.”
gaps_in_A: “venture-backed consumer brands” is not in the supplied update. The finance angle may be smart, but that phrase smuggles in outside context.
“most beverage brands at 120,000 retail doors add more doors, not their own” is plausible, but unsupported by the given facts. Make it a question unless you can prove it.
“The B Corp contrarian angle is the sharpest hook” is a little too confident before the named nonprofit and certification rationale are sourced.
gaps_in_B: “event tickets” is invented. The update says the store runs in-store events, not that it sells tickets.
The first two store angles are too close: “what does owned retail do” and “merch, limited editions, and programming” are different rooms in the same house, not fully separate houses.
Calling the B Corp/$4.2M angle “data” overstates it. A cumulative donation claim with no dates, recipients, or denominator is a proof hunt, not yet a data story.
“The product mix is the story” leans toward marketing-trade filler unless the company can prove merch/events are material revenue, not just launch-day theater.
